abstracts.value: This study evaluated the performance of lumped element kinetic inductance detectors (LEKIDs) fabricated on yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) substrates with yttria concentrations of 9.5%, 13%, and 20% . We focus on the application of LEKIDs in the search for undiscovered double-beta decay on <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$^{94}$</tex-math></inline-formula>Zr and are developing a detector for this purpose. The yttria concentration of YSZ affects its properties, such as ionic conductivity, necessitating analysis of its effects for detector applications. In this work, LEKIDs made with niobium thin films were tested for resonant frequency, quality factor, and temperature-dependent behavior. No significant differences in yttria concentration were observed that would affect LEKID performance. However, temperature-control measurements confirmed a large two-level system contribution, regardless of the yttria concentration.

titles.title: Performance Evaluation of Kinetic Inductance Detector on Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia Substrates With Tuned Yttria Concentrations

abstracts.value: In this article, we present the design of a hybridization and integration of three integrated circuits, each cooled to different cryogenic temperatures. The integration is facilitated by the use of superconducting, and thermally super-insulating multilayer deposits at the interfaces. These circuits are populated with through-silicon vias and hybridized by bumps, enabling up to 14 000 isolated electrical connections between the lower circuit and the upper circuit. This solution will allow the placement of an electronic readout circuit immediately below a detection or a qubit cryogenic circuit, despite the circuits being cooled to different cryogenic temperatures.

titles.title: Direct Hybridization of Integrated Circuits Cooled to Different Cryogenic Temperatures: Device Design

abstracts.value: The CCAT Observatory’s primary science instrument, Prime-Cam, is nearing readiness for deployment to the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope in the Atacama Desert in northern Chile. When fully deployed, Prime-Cam will field approximately 100 000 kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) across seven instrument modules making both broadband and polarimetric measurements. Meanwhile, in-lab characterization of the first CCAT instrument module, a 280-GHz broadband camera fielding over 10 000 KIDs, is currently underway in the test bed instrument Mod-Cam. Both Mod-Cam and Prime-Cam will employ 46-cm-long low-thermal-conductivity flexible circuits (“stripline”) between 4 and 300 K to connect large-format arrays of multiplexed KIDs in each instrument module to readout electronics. The 280-GHz camera currently installed in Mod-Cam uses six of these striplines to read out its over 10 000 detectors. We have examined the thermal and electrical performance of the stripline installed in Mod-Cam in an effort to better optimize the readout chain for deployment in Prime-Cam. We begin by characterizing the oxygen-free high thermal conductivity (OFHC) copper in the stripline traces, allowing for the estimation of thermal loading through these flexible circuits in their configurations in both Mod-Cam and Prime-Cam. We then directly measure the thermal conductivity of the stripline, finding it is best described by <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$kA\,=\,22\pm \text{6}\,T^{0.84\pm 0.09}\,\mathrm{\mu W{\cdot } m{\cdot } K^{-1}}$</tex-math></inline-formula> for temperature ranges of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$6\,\mathrm{K} < T < 20\,\mathrm{K}$</tex-math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$kA\,=\,0.6\pm \text{0.3}\,T^{-0.4\pm 0.1}\,\mathrm{mW{\cdot } m{\cdot }K^{-1}}$</tex-math></inline-formula> for ranges from <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$20\,\mathrm{K}< T < 80\,\mathrm{K}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. Following our thermal characterizations, we report on the transmission and crosstalk properties of the Mod-Cam readout chain, isolating elevated crosstalk to SMP-SMA transition printed circuit boards that interface with the stripline. This finding validates the stripline circuit as a viable high-density cabling option for large-format array readout.

titles.title: CCAT: Flexible Stripline Circuits for Large-Format Kinetic Inductance Detector (KID) Array Readout

abstracts.value: Kinetic inductance detectors are widely used in millimeter- and submillimeter-wave astronomy, benefiting from their fast response and relative ease of fabrication. The GroundBIRD telescope employs microwave kinetic inductance detectors at 145 and 220 GHz to observe the cosmic microwave background. As a ground-based telescope, it is subject to inherent environmental systematics, namely atmospheric emission and thermal fluctuations of the focal plane temperature. This study models resonance frequency shifts induced by each source using calibrated on-site measurements of precipitable water vapor and temperature. Comparison with observational data confirms the validity of the models and identifies atmospheric loading as the dominant contributor to frequency variation under typical observation conditions.

titles.title: GroundBIRD Telescope: Systematics Modelization of MKID Arrays Response

abstracts.value: Scaling astronomical detectors and quantum devices to larger and larger sizes will require more readout lines. A problem with extra readout lines is the complexity and cost of many coaxial cables in parallel. Furthermore, the thermal loading on the coldest stages via thermal conductivity should be kept at a minimum. Delft circuits provides an eight-channel flexible cabling solution based on stripline technology with Ag or NbTi conductors and polyimide dielectric (flexline) as a solution to these problems. However, a compact and light-tight flex-to-chip interface is lacking, and this would be key to unlocking its full scaling and lightweight potential. Here, we present the design and measurements of a flexline to PCB interface for cryogenic detectors. The flexline is connected securely via a spring-loaded pressing tool, ensuring reliable contact even after thermal contraction. To reduce stray radiation, the chip and connector assembly sits in a light-tight setup. The connector spans a width of 20 mm along one edge of the chip, illustrating the compact design. We show that the flexline connector has an insertion loss of –2 dB at 7 GHz using a probe measurement at room temperature. We also demonstrate the connector with a test chip with kinetic inductance detectors in a dilution refrigerator cooled to 40 mK.

titles.title: A Spring-Loaded Chip Interface for Flexible Stripline Cryogenic Readout

abstracts.value: Several experiments are currently competing to directly detect sub-GeV/c<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$^{2}$</tex-math></inline-formula> dark matter through elastic scattering off various target nuclei. Hydrogen-rich materials, such as organic compounds, are promising candidate targets for such experiments due to favorable kinematics. In this article, we present for the first time results obtained with a sugar-based cryogenic particle detector. A sucrose (<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\mathbf {C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}$</tex-math></inline-formula>) monocrystal was instrumented with a neutron transmutation-doped germanium thermistor to detect phonons from particle interactions and was operated in the vicinity of a light detector. Particle interactions in the sugar were observed with associated scintillation light, indicating a possible channel for particle discrimination.

titles.title: The SWEET Project: Probing Sugar Crystals for Direct Dark Matter Searches

abstracts.value: Supercritical CO2 (sCO2 ) is of high interest for compact cooling applications, yet local heat transfer data in millimetric scale horizontal tubes under electronics-relevant conditions remain scarce. This work reports local heat transfer coefficients, pressure drops and temperature-inlet-to-outlet values for CO2 at inlet pressures from 7.5 to 8.5 MPa flowing in a 1 mm horizontal stainless-steel tube with 𝐺 = 2130 kg m−2 s −1 ( ̇𝑚 ≈ 1.8 g s−1 ) and uniform Joule heating over 𝐿ℎ = 0.903 m at 𝑞 = 35 kW m−2 . A calorimetric data reduction based on inlet and outlet conditions is combined with an axial enthalpy integration to express results as a function of bulk enthalpy, thus enabling consistent comparison across inlet temperatures. The obtained heat transfer coefficients span from 10 to 60 kW m−2 K −1 and show a systematic dependence on inlet temperature and pressure through the pseudo-critical region. When the fluid near the wall crosses the pseudo-critical point, a first enhancement is observed, associated with the sharp increase in 𝑐𝑝 , causing the collapse of (𝑇𝑤 −𝑇𝑏 ). The overall pressure drop increases steeply as inlet conditions approach the pseudo-critical temperature, whereas the inlet-to-outlet temperature rise decreases and tends to plateau, highlighting the thermal–hydraulic trade-off in this regime. Additionally, comparison with Petukhov (P) and Krasnoshchekov– Kuraeva–Protopopov (KKP) correlations shows that KKP captures about 85% of data within ±20%, while P overpredicts at high heat transfer coefficients due to the lack of consideration of strong radial property variations. These results provide a benchmark dataset of high Reynolds numbers, low heat flux sCO2 heat transfer in 1 mm horizontal channels and show an improved performance of sCO2 as a local single-phase refrigerant, making it a promising alternative for detector and electronics cooling at warm operating temperatures above 31 𝑜C.

titles.title: Effects of inlet temperature and pressure in sCO2 heat transfer in a 1 mm diameter horizontal tube

abstracts.value: LiteBIRD is an experiment dedicated to the measurement of the primordial <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$B$</tex-math></inline-formula> modes in the cosmic microwave background polarization. This signal is characterized by its faintness, and it is dominated by contamination sources such as galactic foregrounds and instrument systematics. Consequently, the optical system onboard the LiteBIRD satellite must meet several stringent constraints on optical ghosting, and in general, straylight mitigation. The use of microwave absorbing coatings on the 4K-cooled internal surfaces of the telescope enclosure, around the aperture stop and the forebaffle, is required to ensure straylight suppression. Therefore, a selection of materials with suitable optical and thermo-mechanical properties is required. For the LiteBIRD absorbers, a baseline material recipe was selected, based on a mixture of epoxy resins and conductive loading powders. The design features a 3-D textured broadband nonreflective surface, which has been developed to minimize reflections in the 89–448 GHz band. A variation of the design is also under study for the purpose of extending the straylight mitigation toward the lower frequency (40–448 GHz). This will be achieved taking into account the necessary design variations to accommodate the challenging constraints of the mass allocation for the telescope.

titles.title: Optical Characterization of Microwave Absorbers for Straylight Suppression in the LiteBIRD Telescopes

abstracts.value: X-ray microcalorimeter space missions require an anti-coincidence detector to mitigate background events from Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs). These high-energy particles mimic an X-ray signal by depositing energy in the microcalorimeter absorber, with the amount proportional to their track length. An anti-coincidence detector, positioned below the main microcalorimeter array, identifies these background events and should respond quickly to a GCR signal, has a low threshold and high dynamic range, and uses a similar readout scheme as the main detector array. For the proposed Line Emission Mapper (LEM) X-ray probe concept, a W and Al-based athermal phonon sensor design, originally developed for the Cryogenic Dark Matter Search, was adapted to cover a large Si substrate (14 cm<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$^{2}$</tex-math></inline-formula>) with 12 parallel networks of these sensors. This initial prototype for the LEM mission was developed in collaboration with SLAC and Northwestern University, and tested at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. The prototype demonstrated a combination of low threshold, high dynamic range, and millimeter-scale position discrimination, far exceeding all mission requirements. At the same time, detector modeling efforts were undertaken to understand the rich datasets produced by the prototype. In this work, we expand upon these modeling capabilities to explore new anti-coincidence particle detection designs enabled by the high performance of the LEM prototype. Using G4CMP, an add-on framework to Geant4 for phonon and charge transport in cryogenic detectors, we model the athermal phonon signals generated by GCR events and their collection as quasiparticles in the sensor network. We consider alternative sensor network layouts to maximize GCR event position discrimination, which could reduce false-coincidence events by localizing event rejection in the main array.

titles.title: Simulation Driven Design of a Cryogenic Anti-Coincidence Detector for X-Ray Microcalorimeter Space Missions

abstracts.value: We propose that early Super Massive Black Holes (SMBHs) grow at an enhanced Eddington rate facilitated by rotation. Recent theoretical work suggests that rotating Black Holes (BHs) can produce winds or jets carrying electric currents. These currents are driven by a pE−2 momentum spectrum of protons and anti-protons, which can reach EeV energies for near-maximal rotation — independent of the BHs mass. This electric current generated in the ergo-region leads to rapid collisions producing anti-particles and lots of pions. The associated electron population suffers extreme losses in the magnetic field observed, so that the protons, anti-protons, neutrons, anti-neutrons and pions altogether, carry a much larger mass/energy per electron than a single proton, while charge is conserved.This factor can be estimated, depends on the spin of the BH, and allows a significant enhancement of Eddington limited accretion. This effect is proposed to explain the rapid growth of early SMBHs observed by James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The prediction is that these SMBHs rotate rapidly. When compared with cosmological simulations of structure evolution with SMBH formation and evolution without allowing for BH rotation, a second testable prediction is that the gravitational waves produced in ensuing SMBH mergers are enhanced due to high rotation, with ensuing increased total mass.

titles.title: Electric discharges: Early growth of super-massive black holes

abstracts.value: The next-generation DIRC (xpDIRC) represents a novel detector geometry concept currently being developed for advanced particle identification systems in high-energy physics experiments. Building upon the high-performance DIRC (hpDIRC) designed for the ePIC detector at the Electron-Ion Collider, the xpDIRC introduces a hybrid optical architecture that combines enhanced focusing optics, a wide plate light guide, and a compact expansion volume. Comprehensive Geant4 simulations demonstrate that the xpDIRC hybrid geometry achieves state-of-the-art performance in π/K separation across the entire range of operation.

abstracts.value: Ce3+–doped gadolinium-based fluoro–oxide (GFO) glass was developed for prospective high-energy physics (HEP) experiment applications. The minimum ionizing particle (MIP) response and timing characteristics of GFO glasses coupled with a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM, 3*3 mm2) were investigated using a cosmic-ray (muon) coincidence setup. The MIP response of a 1 cm-thick glass is 142.1 ± 1.7 p.e., satisfying the criteria for hadron calorimeter applications. As the thickness increases, the MIP responses decrease to 112.7 ± 0.4 (2 cm-thick) and 76.8 ± 1.4 p.e./cm (4 cm-thick). Additionally, Cosmic-ray-induced scintillation shows a dominant slow decay component of ∼500 ns which increases with glass thickness. In this work, appropriately increasing the trigger area remains an effective method to improve the trigger efficiency. According to Monte Carlo simulation, the MIP responses are close to the experimental values, maintaining errors below 6%. The simulated MIP response reaches a maximum value of 361.7 ± 2.7 p.e. for a 5 cm thickness, owing to the short attenuation length of GFO glass which leads to significant photon absorption. Therefore, enhancing its light attenuation length to reduce light loss during internal transmission is currently a critical objective.

titles.title: Cosmic ray experiment and simulation of Ce$^{3+}$–doped high gadolinium-based fluoro–oxide glass scintillators

abstracts.value: CLLBC is an inorganic detector material of interest for several application spaces, including non-proliferation. The multi-modal aspect of CLLBC, sensitive to gamma-rays, thermal neutrons, and fast neutrons, makes it particularly interesting for Arms Control. To explore the utility of CLLBC for Arms Control, a detector needs to be characterized and optimized to test its performance in relevant scenarios. In addition, validation through simulation is vital for exploring specific use cases for the detector. In this work, a detector with ⌀⌀ 38 mm ×38 mm cylinder CLLBC crystal is used to study pulse shape discrimination of thermal neutrons and gamma-rays, as well as the timing and resolution of the gamma-ray signal for most optimized performance. Additionally, the intrinsic detection efficiency to gamma-rays is characterized through multiple experimental measurements and a high fidelity MCNP model of this detector that was developed and validated against several gamma-ray sources. The characterization of the fast neutrons will be presented in a future article.

titles.title: Characterization and optimization of a CLLBC detector

abstracts.value: The High Energy Photon Source (HEPS) is a fourth-generation synchrotron light source located in Beijing, China. To achieve ultra-low emittance, a compact hybrid seven-bend achromat lattice design has been adopted for the storage ring, together with high-gradient quadrupoles, combined-function magnets and longitudinal gradient dipoles. Magnetic cross-talk can degrade machine performance and therefore must be carefully evaluated. To this end, several methods based on one-dimensional and three-dimensional magnetic fields data are used to model the cross-talk effect of magnets in the HEPS storage ring. This paper introduces the detailed modelling approaches and investigates the impact of cross-talk on the linear optics of the HEPS storage ring.

titles.title: Modelling of the magnetic cross-talk effect of the HEPS storage ring

Sustainable sandwich panels from upcycled aluminium cans, galvanised 
steel, and biobased adhesive

Arthur Santos Longati a , Rodrigo José da Silva a,b,c,d,* , Leandro José da Silva a ,  
Júlio Cesar dos Santos a , Hulisses Boneti Marcon a , Michael Jenkins e , Fabrizio Scarpa d ,  
Tulio Hallak Panzera a,**

a Centre for Innovation and Technology in Composite Materials (CITeC), Federal University of São João del-Rei (UFSJ), São João del-Rei, Brazil
b CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, R&D Programme EP-DT, Geneva, Switzerland
c German Aerospace Center (DLR), Institute of Structures and Design, Stuttgart, Germany
d Bristol Composites Institute, School of Civil, Aerospace and Design Engineering (CADE), University of Bristol, Bristol, United Kingdom
e School of Metallurgy & Materials, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom

A R T I C L E  I N F O

Keywords:
Sandwich panel
Circular honeycomb core
Reused aluminium
Three-point bending

A B S T R A C T

This study explores the design of sandwich panels using recycled aluminium can rings as the core material. The 
panels are also made with galvanised steel face sheets and a plant-based castor oil adhesive. To assess different 
configurations, two core architectures (cubic and hexagonal) are investigated, and the steel face sheets are tested 
both with and without sanding treatment to increase the roughness of the bonding surfaces. The structural 
properties of the panels are characterised using three-point bending tests, following the ASTM standards C393 
and D7250, as well as the RJS Method (an approach to measure the homogenised flexural modulus of sandwich 
structures). Optimal results are obtained for the hexagonal packing for the core architecture associated with skins 
without sanding: a maximum load of 415 N, representing a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N⋅m and a mean 
homogenised flexural modulus of 2143 MPa, demonstrating a viable and sustainable method for using 
aluminium cans as a core material for secondary structural applications in the construction and transportation 
industries. Failure analysis reveals that core–skin debonding is the primary cause of structural collapse. This 
indicates that interfacial adhesion is the critical design constraint for these recycled-aluminium sandwich panels.

1. Introduction

Due to increasing global demand for technology and growing climate 
change concerns, engineering and materials science have become 
crucial disciplines for meeting global sustainability challenges and of
fering technologies that balance technical performance, economic 
viability, and environmental responsibility: the three pillars of sustain
ability [1]. The Brundtland Report of 1987 formalised sustainability as 
"development that meets the needs of the present without compromising 
the ability of future generations to meet their own needs." A project is 
considered sustainable if it addresses the three dimensions of sustain
ability: environmental, social, and economic. This requires the model to 
be environmentally responsible, economically viable, and socially rele
vant, serving the interests of both society and the productive sector [2].

To meet sustainability goals, industries like the automotive, naval, 
aeronautical, and aerospace sectors are seeking to develop technologies 
that use lightweight, efficient, and low-cost structures. These charac
teristics are found in sandwich panels, which are used in structural ap
plications ranging from secondary to high-performance [3,4]. Sandwich 
panels represent a significant advance in engineering and materials 
science because they offer a unique combination of low density and high 
stiffness. This is achieved by combining two thin, rigid outer layers (face 
sheets) with a lightweight, thicker core [5].

The increasing demand for sustainable engineering solutions drives 
the development of sandwich panels featuring cores derived from 
recyclable or renewable materials [6,7]. Recent investigations demon
strate promising structural configurations using industrial and urban 
waste, including bottle caps, bamboo rings, and natural fibres [8–11].

Unlike conventional configurations, the discrete nature of the cylindri
cal rings promotes localised instability and progressive collapse in a 
more controlled and distributed manner, thereby enhancing energy 
dissipation. This behaviour remains consistent with instability-driven 
mechanisms reported for thin-walled tubular structures, while high
lighting the additional design flexibility provided by segmented 
geometries.

Additionally, alternative geometries have been explored [8], 
including tubular honeycomb (TH) cells, one of the most recently 
developed core topologies. THs have been used in various applications, 
from supporting oil transportation infrastructure to energy absorption 
panels [12]. Research by Oruganti and Goshi [13] demonstrated that the 
geometric constraints of these cylindrical structures provide them with 
intrinsic stiffness and increased strength.

More broadly, thin-walled cylindrical structures serve as efficient 
energy-absorbing systems due to their progressive collapse mechanisms 
and favourable strength-to-weight ratios. For instance, nested multi- 
tube configurations exhibit significant capacity for energy absorption 
under quasi-static loading, which highlights the mechanical efficiency of 
thin-walled cylindrical architectures [14]. Similarly, investigations into 
recycled beverage cans demonstrate that thin-walled tubular elements 
exhibit promising crashworthiness and energy absorption behaviour, 
reinforcing their potential application in sustainable structural systems 
[15].

This work presents an innovative approach by reusing abundant 
waste aluminium cans as a honeycomb tubular core material, thereby 
avoiding the energy consumption and emissions associated with tradi
tional recycling. These cores are easily created by cutting the cans into 
rings. The sandwich panels comprise galvanised steel face sheets and a 
core of reused aluminium can rings, bonded with a bio-based castor oil- 
derived polyurethane adhesive. These rings are arranged in both cubic 
and hexagonal packing configurations to form the core structure. These 
panels are intended for lightweight structural applications where the 
stiffness-to-weight ratio and energy absorption are critical. Potential 
applications include aerospace and aviation secondary structures (e.g., 
interior partitions), architectural systems (e.g., mezzanine flooring), 
marine structures (e.g., bulkheads), and transportation systems (e.g., 
ramps and tailgates for rail vehicles). Furthermore, the design shows 
potential for high-performance furniture and cabinetry.

The mechanical properties of these panels are evaluated using a 
three-point bending test, following the RJS1 Method [16] and the ASTM 
standards C393 and D7250 [17,18]. This analysis assesses the structural 
feasibility and load-bearing capacity of these sustainable secondary so
lutions for applications in the construction and transportation 
industries.

2. Methodology

2.1. Materials

The sandwich panel consists of 0.53 mm-thick galvanised steel skins 
and a tubular honeycomb core made from reused aluminium rings. The 
rings, each with a thickness of 0.14 mm and a height of 15 mm, are 
arranged in either a hexagonal (Fig. 1a) or cubic (Fig. 1b) packing shape. 
A 1.5 mm thick biobased castor-oil adhesive is used to bond the skins to 
the core, as properly addressed further in the text.

2.2. Characterisation and manufacture

A tensile test is performed on the galvanised steel and aluminium 
sheets in the circumferential direction, following ASTM E8 [19], to 
obtain the elastic modulus, ultimate strength, and ultimate strain. The 

tests are conducted using an Instron testing machine equipped with a 50 
kN load cell, at crosshead speeds of 6 mm/min (galvanised steel) and 0.5 
mm/min (aluminium). A mechanical extensometer is employed for 
strain measurement (Fig. 2). The mechanical properties of the castor-oil 
adhesive were sourced from previous research [20].

The bulk densities of the materials were determined as 2.61 ± 0.23 
g/cm³ for aluminium and 0.98 ± 0.11 g/cm³ for the castor-oil polymer, 
based on the experimental research reported in [20]. The mean bulk 
density of galvanised steel (8.03±0.05 g/cm³) is obtained by the ratio of 
mass and volume measured using a precision scale (accurate to 0.01 g) 
and digital calliper (accurate to 0.01 mm).

The sandwich panels are manufactured through a multi-step process 
designed, as depicited in Fig. 3, to ensure proper assembly and curing. 
First, galvanised steel sheets (185 × 415 mm²) are cut to size according 
to ASTM C393 [17], which specifies a minimum length of two times the 
width and a minimum width of three core cells. To prevent slippage 
during bending tests, an additional safety margin is included. The sur
faces are degreased with detergent and rinsed to remove contaminants. 
Next, the aluminium rings are cut using a Makita® marble saw to ensure 
uniform and precise dimensions. A subset of the galvanised steel sheets 
is sanded on both sides with 100-grit sandpaper to evaluate the effect of 
surface treatment, followed by the same degreasing and washing. The 
assembly process begins by placing the steel skins into a polystyrene 
plate mould covered with a film to prevent resin leakage. The adhesive

veg® (Brazil). The components are mixed at a mass ratio of 1.2:1 (pol
yol:isocyanate) for one minute and then uniformly applied to the steel 
sheets, resulting in an adhesive spread rate of approximately 1700 g⋅m⁻² 
and an adhesive layer thickness of roughly 1.5 mm. Previous in
vestigations by the same research group [16] indicated that this specific 
thickness yields the optimum mechanical performance for the bonded 
assembly.

The cut aluminium rings (15 ± 0.1 mm high) are then arranged side- 
by-side on the adhesive-coated surface, forming either a cubic or hex
agonal core packing. All four panel conditions (cubic/hexagonal core 
with/without sanded skins) are fabricated on the same day to maintain 
consistency. The mould is then covered with a wooden plate and com
pacted at a uniaxial pressure of 0.64 kPa for 24 h at room temperature 
(22±2 ◦C). This compaction ensured proper bonding and consolidation. 
After demoulding, the second side of the panel is bonded using the same 
process. Finally, the completed sandwich panel is cured for 14 days at an 
ambient temperature of 22±2 ◦C to allow for the full development of its 
mechanical properties and stability.

The fabrication process and subsequent testing are randomised ac
cording to a full factorial Design of Experiments (DoE) to investigate the 
effects of core packing and face sanding on the three-point bending 
properties of aluminium-tubular-core panels. The main factors and their 
levels are (i) core packing (cubic and hexagonal) and (ii) skin treatment 
(with and without 100-grit sandpaper), leading to 22 design as shown in 
Table 1. DoE is analysed using the statistical software Minitab® [21].

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Properties of panel components

Table 2 presents the mean properties of the sandwich panel com
ponents. The mechanical properties values reported for the biobased 
adhesive were obtained from Ref. [20], which investigated similar ma
terials and components to those employed in the present study. The 
tensile modulus of the reused aluminium core is approximately 22% of 
the modulus of elasticity of galvanised steel. Furthermore, the adhesive's 
deformation capacity is 28 times greater than that of the core material. 
These characteristics highlight the complementary roles of the materials 
for a sandwich structure design: rigid skins combined with a less rigid 
but lightweight core structure, with an adhesive layer more ductile than 
the core, which allows for greater deformability.

3.2. Al-tubular core panels: three-point bending properties

Table 3 presents the mean values and standard deviations for the 
following response variables: equivalent density, maximum load, 
experimental flexural modulus, core shear modulus, and modulus of 
toughness. For each property, the best-performing values are under
lined, while the second-best values are in italics. The equivalent density 
of the panels is defined as the ratio between mass and homogenised 
volume. The low variability in equivalent density across all tested con
ditions and replicates, evidenced by minimal standard deviations, 
demonstrates a robust raw materials preparation and manufacturing 
process. Condition C4 demonstrates superior performance across 
approximately 80% of the properties analysed. The only exception is the 
modulus of toughness, for which the highest values are consistently 
observed in configurations with cubic packing, particularly in condition 
C1.

Fig. 5 displays typical force-displacement and mean stress-strain 
curves for each experimental condition, as obtained using the homog
enisation concept from the RJS method [16,24,25]. Condition C4, which 
consists of a hexagonal core with untreated skins, exhibited the highest 
maximum force (~ 415 N), corresponding to an ultimate mean stress of 
approximately 4.25 MPa and a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N⋅m. 
This behaviour suggests that the larger contact area and inherently more 
stable geometry of the hexagonal cell promoted a more uniform load 
distribution, thus increasing the material's resistance, as previously 
discussed. The next highest values are observed in the hexagonal 
configuration with sanded skins (~340 N / ~3.6 MPa), followed by the 
cubic core with sanded skins (~325 N / ~3.4 MPa), and the cubic 
configuration with unsanded skins (~320 N / ~3.3 MPa).

The post-failure load-carrying capacity observed for the cubic 
configuration with skin treatment (blue curve in Fig. 5) indicates the 
activation of specific deformation mechanisms within the tubular core. 
As the load is applied approximately at the panel centre, directly coin
ciding with the core cells, initial failure does not lead to immediate 
structural collapse. Rather, the progressive deformation of the rings 
suggests local rearrangement and partial densification of the cellular 
structure, which enables sustaining additional load following the initial 
peak.

3.3. Al-tubular core panels: statistical analysis of properties

Table 4 summarises the statistical analysis conducted using Design of 
Experiment (DoE) and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) tools in Minitab 
software. The R2 values (>74%) confirm that the statistical model has a 
satisfactory fit to the experimental data. Additionally, the P-valueAD 

(Anderson-Darling test) and P-valueB (Bartlett test) are presented; values 
greater than 0.05 for both tests indicate data normality and homoge
neity, respectively. These conditions validate the use of ANOVA.

The variables P-valueT, P-valueP, and P-valueTP indicate the signifi
cance of the factors: face treatment, core packing, and the interaction 
between these two factors. A P-value ≤0.05 (in bold, Table 4) suggests 
that the factor or interaction has a statistically significant effect on the 
response variable. P-values (Table 4, highlighted in bold) shall be 
visualised and evaluated using the effect plots presented in Fig. 6. Spe
cifically, when an interaction effect is determined to be statistically 
significant, the separate interpretation of the main effects is typically not 
performed.

The core packing factor significantly affects all properties except 
equivalent density, meaning density does not differ between conditions. 
It's also important to note that the maximum load and flexural strength 
are the only properties influenced by the face treatment. This is likely 
because the treatment enhances the interaction and contact area be
tween the adhesive and the facesheets, which in turn improves the 

panel's performance during plastic deformation. Additionally, the 
interaction between these two factors significantly impacts all the 
modulus properties. The main effect plots and their interactions for each 
response variable, where significant, are shown in Fig. 6(a-e).

The main effect plots for the maximum load are presented in Fig. 6a. 
Skin treatment negatively impacts the maximum load, resulting in an 
8.7% reduction (from ~351 N to ~323 N). Conversely, adopting a 
hexagonal core packing significantly improved the maximum load by 
7.4% (from ~323 N to ~347 N) over the cubic configuration. As 
depicted in Fig. 6b, a comparable effect is evidenced for the flexural 
strength. The optimal performance, with the highest flexural strength, is 
obtained from panels combining untreated skins with the hexagonal 
core. This enhancement is attributed to the hexagonal geometry pro
moting closer packing and reduced gaps between core caps, thereby 
strengthening cell interaction and facilitating a more uniform distribu
tion of internal stresses.

The interaction effect concerning the flexural modulus is delineated 
in Fig. 6c. A statistically significant increase in the flexural modulus 
(approximately 1950 MPa) is attained when utilising hexagonal packing 
compared with the cubic packing (≈1200 MPa). This enhanced perfor
mance is consistent with the advantages of the hexagonal configuration 
in promoting superior volumetric packing and structural integrity.

3.4. Al-tubular core panels: modes of failure

Fig. 7(a–d) illustrates the behaviour of the sandwich panels during 
the three-point bending test for the four conditions proposed in the study 
(C1–C4). The skins of the panels remain intact, even under maximum 
tensile and compressive loads. However, detachment of the lower skin is 
observed in all sandwich panels. Although the panels' construction is 
symmetrical, the manual manufacturing process and its possible varia
tions occasionally result in an unbalanced deflection curvature. This 
behaviour can also generate a heterogeneous stress distribution, over
loading certain regions and consequently causing detachment of the 
adhesive interface outside the beam's central region.

Some samples from conditions C3 and C4 exhibit not only the 
detachment of the lower skin but also a longitudinal rupture of the core 
cells in the out-of-plane direction (see Figs. 7c’–d’). It is noteworthy that 
these conditions withstand the highest bending loads. It is believed that 
the core crack is caused by tensile stresses at the interface with the 
bottom face, which promotes the emergence and propagation of the 
crack. Indirect compressive forces generated in the out-of-plane direc
tion may further contribute to the crack propagation and the opening of 
the tear.

In addition to the core crack, some samples demonstrate a 'counter- 
curvature,' as illustrated in Fig. 7c. This behaviour is attributed to the 
buckling of the upper face, which causes the structure to rotate. This 
rotation subsequently leads to the detachment of the core's lower face. 
Note the lifting of the rings, which indicates an out-of-plane force 
generated by the structure's rotation during the imbalance caused by the 
upper face's buckling.

From a structural perspective, these observations align with the non- 
classical response characteristic of a segmented, friction-dominated core 
system. The discrete ring-based topology, exacerbated by the absence of 
chemical bonding between core elements, results in a lack of transverse 
shear continuity. Consequently, load transfer is governed by localised 
contacts and frictional interactions rather than a continuous stress field, 
which induces stress concentrations and non-uniform deformation pat
terns. This mechanical state inherently suppresses classical failure 

modes, such as core crushing or face wrinkling, favouring instead 
interfacial instability, progressive loss of contact, and localised collapse 
mechanisms.

The experimental results demonstrate that the failure of the pro
posed sandwich panels is governed by interfacial core–skin debonding, 
rather than core crushing or face-sheet yielding. Although the tubular 
core exhibited sufficient compressive stability and the skins remained 
predominantly within the elastic-plastic regime, separation initiated at 
the interface and propagated rapidly under flexural loading. This failure 
mode indicates that the adhesion between the tubular aluminium core 
and the face sheets constitutes the primary structural constraint for the 
current configuration. Consequently, from a design perspective, 
enhancing the bonding strategy, through optimised adhesive selection, 
surface functionalisation, or mechanical interlocking, is a critical pri
ority for increasing the load-bearing capacity of these recycled- 
aluminium sandwich structures.

In this context, applying the RJS homogenisation method, which 
assumes the core makes a negligible contribution to the global flexural 
stiffness, provides a reasonable approximation for the current configu
ration. Although the core comprises metallic tubular elements, the 
experimental response indicates that deformation is predominantly 
shear-dominated, with failure occurring at the core–skin interface rather 
than through core crushing. Consistent with findings in [16], a thickness 
of 1.5 mm yielded the most favourable results. This thickness enhances 
in-plane interlocking between adjacent rings, thereby restricting relative 
movement and increasing the in-plane shear resistance of the core as
sembly. However, its influence on the out-of-plane structural response 
remains limited. This aligns with the observed failure mode, which was 
governed by core–skin debonding, indicating that structural failure was 
driven by out-of-plane separation rather than in-plane shear of the 
tubular lattice.

4. Conclusions

This study investigated the mechanical performance of Al-arched- 
core sandwich panels (support span: 370 mm, width: 185 mm) under

three-point bending. The panels achieved a maximum load of up to 415 
N representing a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N.m. The measured 
experimental flexural modulus averages 2163 MPa, noting that the 
theoretical flexural modulus under pure bending is projected to reach 35 
GPa under large spans. The hexagonal core packing significantly en
hances the panel's overall flexural strength and stiffness. Conversely, the 
cubic core configuration yields the highest modulus of toughness under 
both skin conditions. This superior toughness stems from the cubic 
packing's enhanced energy absorption capacity prior to fracture, likely 
due to a more gradual redistribution of internal stresses and a less abrupt 
failure mechanism. This suggests the cubic configuration is the more 
advantageous choice for applications demanding toughness (e.g., 
impact or dynamic loading), even with a potential reduction in struc
tural stiffness. The primary failure mechanism across all panels is 
detachment at the core-skin interface, with subsequent failure modes 
including ring rupture and upper face buckling in specific cases. Sta
tistical analysis confirms significant interaction effects between design 
factors, demonstrating that mechanical performance is dictated not by a 
single parameter but by the integrated set of geometric, material, and 
procedural specifications. This necessitates a systemic approach for the 
development of these sandwich structures. In summary, sandwich 
panels fabricated from a core of reused aluminium rings, biobased ad
hesive, and galvanised steel skins represent a promising, sustainable 
alternative that satisfies industrial demands for lightness, strength, and 
environmental responsibility.

The results demonstrate that the structural performance of the 
developed sandwich panels is limited neither by core compressive 
strength nor face-sheet yielding; rather, it is governed by interfacial 
core–skin debonding, which consistently dictated the failure process. 
This finding identifies the core–skin interface as the critical design 
parameter for the future optimisation of sandwich panels fabricated 
with upcycled aluminium-can tubular cores. Consequently, enhancing 
interfacial bond integrity is expected to yield a significant increase in the 
structural efficiency and load-bearing capacity of the proposed 
architecture.

abstracts.value: This study explores the design of sandwich panels using recycled aluminium can rings as the core material. The panels are also made with galvanised steel face sheets and a plant-based castor oil adhesive. To assess different configurations, two core architectures (cubic and hexagonal) are investigated, and the steel face sheets are tested both with and without sanding treatment to increase the roughness of the bonding surfaces. The structural properties of the panels are characterised using three-point bending tests, following the ASTM standards C393 and D7250, as well as the RJS Method (an approach to measure the homogenised flexural modulus of sandwich structures). Optimal results are obtained for the hexagonal packing for the core architecture associated with skins without sanding: a maximum load of 415 N, representing a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N·m and a mean homogenised flexural modulus of 2143 MPa, demonstrating a viable and sustainable method for using aluminium cans as a core material for secondary structural applications in the construction and transportation industries. Failure analysis reveals that core–skin debonding is the primary cause of structural collapse. This indicates that interfacial adhesion is the critical design constraint for these recycled-aluminium sandwich panels.

titles.title: Sustainable sandwich panels from upcycled aluminium cans, galvanised steel, and biobased adhesive

abstracts.value: This paper investigates whether it is possible to have a Turing machine that is able to compute the minimum (or fundamental) period of a given periodic computable continuous function. It is shown that for every periodic computable continuous function <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\boldsymbol{f}$</tex-math> </inline-formula>, its fundamental period is always a computable number. Therefore, there always exists a specific Turing machine, which depends on <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\boldsymbol{f}$</tex-math> </inline-formula>, for computing the period of <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\boldsymbol{f}$</tex-math> </inline-formula>. Nevertheless, it is also shown that there exists no universal algorithm on a Turing machine that is able to compute the period for all functions having periods that are smaller than a given upper bound. This result is established even for a class of nonlinear operators that compute a bounded deviation from the minimal period. It is shown that these operators are not even Banach–Mazur computable and therefore fail to satisfy even the weakest computability requirements known from the theory of digital computation.

titles.title: Period Finding for Continuous Functions Cannot Be Automated on Turing Machines

abstracts.value: We study space-bounded communication complexity for unitary implementation in distributed quantum processors, where we restrict the number of qubits per processor to ensure practical relevance and technical non-triviality. We model distributed quantum processors using distributed quantum circuits with nonlocal two-qubit gates, defining the distributed communication complexity of a unitary as the minimum number of such nonlocal gates required for its realization, up to permutations of data qubit positions. Our contributions are twofold. First, for general <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$n$ </tex-math></inline-formula>-qubit unitaries, we improve upon the trivial <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$O(4^{n})$ </tex-math></inline-formula> communication bound. With <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$k$ </tex-math></inline-formula> pairwise-connected processors (each having <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$n/k$ </tex-math></inline-formula> data qubits and <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$m$ </tex-math></inline-formula> ancillas), we prove the communication complexity satisfies <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$O\left ({ \max \{4^{(1-1/k)n - m}, n\}}\right)$ </tex-math></inline-formula> —e.g., <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$O(2^{n})$ </tex-math></inline-formula> when <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$m=0$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$k=2$ </tex-math></inline-formula>—and show this upper bound is tight. We also extend the analysis to approximation and general topology models. Second, for special unitaries, we demonstrate that both Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and Clifford circuits admit linear upper bounds on communication complexity within the exact model. This outperforms the trivial quadratic communication complexity that applies to these two unitaries. In the approximation model, QFT’s communication complexity reduces drastically from linear to logarithmic, while Clifford circuits still require at least linear communication. These results provide fundamental insights into optimizing communication for distributed quantum unitary implementation, advancing the feasibility of large-scale DQC systems.

titles.title: Communication Complexity of Distributed Unitary Synthesis

abstracts.value: Encoding quantum information in a quantum error correction (QEC) code offers protection against decoherence and enhances the fidelity of qubits and gate operations. One of the fundamental challenges of QEC is to construct codes with asymptotically good parameters, i.e. a non-vanishing rate and relative minimum distance. Recently, bivariate bicycle (BB) codes have emerged as a promising candidate for such compact memory, though the exact tradeoff of the code parameters $[[n,k,d]]$ remained unknown. Despite recent proof that BB codes are asymptotically bad, they serve as candidate codes for near-term QEC beyond the surface code. In this article, we provide a more concrete characterisation of the performance of BB codes by identifying sufficient and necessary conditions for these codes to exist, using the fact that they are generated by finite field trinomials, and writing explicit formulas to calculate their code dimension by identifying common roots of these trinomials, using Gröbner bases.

titles.title: Existence and Characterization of Bivariate Bicycle Codes

We show that <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\widetilde {\Theta } (k) $ </tex-math></inline-formula> samples of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\rho $ </tex-math></inline-formula> are sufficient and necessary to simultaneously estimate all the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$k$ </tex-math></inline-formula> values. This means that estimating all the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$k$ </tex-math></inline-formula> values is almost as easy as estimating only one of them, <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\mathrm {tr}( \mathcal {O}\rho ^{k}) $ </tex-math></inline-formula>. abstracts.value:
The existence of $k$ -uniform states has been a widely studied problem due to their applications in several quantum information tasks and their close relation to combinatorial objects like Latin squares and orthogonal arrays. With the machinery of quantum enumerators and linear programming, we establish several improved non-existence results and bounds on $k$ -uniform states.

First, for any fixed $l\geq 1$ and $q\geq 2$ , we show that there exists a constant $c$ such that $(\left \lfloor { n/2}\right \rfloor -l)$ -uniform states in $(\mathbb {C}^{q})^{\otimes n}$ do not exist when $n\geq cq^{2}+o(q^{2})$ . The constant $c$ equals 4 when $l=1$ and 6 when $l=2$ , which generalizes Scott’s bound (2004) for $l=0$ .

Second, when $n$ is sufficiently large, we show that there exists a constant $\theta \lt 1/2$ for each $q \le 9$ , such that $k$ -uniform states in $(\mathbb {C}^{q})^{\otimes n}$ exist only when $k\leq \theta n$ . In particular, this provides the first bound (to the best of our knowledge) of $k$ for $4\leq q\leq 9$ and confirms a conjecture posed by Shi et al. (2023) when $q=5$ in a stronger form.

Finally, with numerical methods, we improve the shadow bounds given by Shi et al. (2023) by a constant for $q = 3,4,5$ and small $n$ . When $q=4$ , our results can update some bounds listed in the code tables maintained by Grassl (2007–2024).

titles.title: Linear Programming Bounds on --Uniform States

abstracts.value: This paper extends the Schrödinger quantum field—a wave function treated as a fundamental quantum field describing particle states and probabilities—to a fully relativistic framework within Parametrized Relativistic Quantum Theory (PRQT). A hallmark of parametrized theories is the use of an invariant evolution parameter, which addresses key conceptual challenges in standard quantum field theory (QFT). Feynman's path integral formulation is reviewed to illustrate the historical role of such parameters in early QFT developments. We then present a variational approach, based on the Pavšič–Barut action principle with a parametrized Lagrangian density, to derive field equations that naturally incorporate the invariant evolution parameter and yield a mass operator. The consistency of this formalism with physical measurements is demonstrated through applications to the Stueckelberg equation, including its implications for particle trajectories and mass states. The potential for resolving Standard Model anomalies is discussed.

titles.title: Extending the Schrödinger quantum field to parametrized quantum field theory: A variational approach using the Pavšič–Barut action

abstracts.value: As we move further into the second quantum revolution, it becomes increasingly important to teach modern ideas such as decoherence and to provide practical training on quantum computers. In this work, we illustrate how quantum decoherence channels can be introduced into instruction and how one can simulate these quantum channels on quantum computers. We focus on the decoherence of a single spin, because it is the simplest case to consider. Using the IBM Quantum Platform, we examine depolarizing, amplitude damping, dephasing, and thermalizing channels. These channels are first described in terms of Lindblad operators and then they are converted into quantum circuits that require mid-circuit resets. This hands-on approach to decoherence will help students learn practical concepts required for quantum information science.

titles.title: Teaching decoherence by simulating quantum channels on quantum computers

abstracts.value: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> We construct the quantum double ramification (DR) hierarchy associated with the Gromov–Witten theory of elliptic curves. We use results of Oberdieck and Pixton on the intersection numbers of the DR cycle, the Gromov–Witten classes of the elliptic curve, and the Hodge class , together with vanishing results for to produce a closed, modular expression for the resulting integrable hierarchy. It is the first explicit nontrivial example of a quantum integrable hierarchy from a cohomological field theory containing fermionic fields, which correspond to the odd classes in the cohomology of the elliptic curve.

abstracts.value: Maintaining high-quality detector data is essential for achieving the scientific objectives of the Short-Baseline Neutrino (SBN) Program at Fermilab. Current data quality monitoring (DQM) procedures rely primarily on threshold-based metrics and manual inspection of detector monitoring plots, making the detection of subtle or gradually developing anomalies both time-consuming and dependent on expert interpretation. This project developed and evaluated a machine-learning workflow for automatically identifying anomalous photomultiplier tube (PMT) channels in the Short-Baseline Near Detector (SBND) using optical-hit amplitude data. A Python-based analysis program was developed to process ROOT files, extract statistical features describing individual PMT amplitude distributions, and generate feature vectors for anomaly detection. These features were used to train an Isolation Forest model using data representing normal detector operation. The trained model was subsequently applied to independent detector runs to identify channels exhibiting statistically unusual behavior relative to the learned reference response. To support expert interpretation, the workflow generated complementary diagnostic products, including anomaly score distributions, normalized amplitude comparisons, decision-tree visualizations, and principal component analysis (PCA) projections. This project demonstrated the feasibility of integrating unsupervised machine learning into detector data-quality monitoring and developed a complete workflow for automated PMT performance assessment to aid expert-driven review. Beyond its technical contributions, the VFP appointment fostered a research collaboration between Aurora University and Fermilab and provided direct workforce development benefits by training the visiting faculty member in detector-scale machine-learning methods that are now being incorporated into undergraduate coursework and research. The methodology developed here provides a foundation for future applications to ProtoDUNE and other liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) detectors, contributing to ongoing efforts to improve detector reliability, reduce manual monitoring requirements, and enable scalable data quality monitoring for future large-scale neutrino experiments, including the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE).

titles.title: Machine Learning-Based Anomaly Detection for PMT Data Quality Monitoring in the SBN and DUNE

abstracts.value: Nonreciprocal conversion is essential for protecting sources and enabling unidirectional signal routing in photonic, phononic, electronic, and quantum systems, yet conventional implementations often rely on magnetic bias that can be difficult to integrate on chip. We propose a magnet-free scheme for frequency-domain nonreciprocity based on sequential, time-gated modulation in a three-mode system. By activating interactions in a fixed temporal order, the forward and reverse frequency-conversion pathways acquire unequal dwell times in a lossy intermediate mode, producing strong nonreciprocity without requiring nonlinearities or magnetic materials. Using harmonic-balance and Dyson-Born expansions, we derive an analytical expression for the isolation ratio and show that breaking time-reversal symmetry alone is insufficient to produce isolation in this scheme: Dissipation in the intermediate mode is necessary, and the isolation is maximized at a finite loss. The resulting framework identifies how duty cycles, modulation frequency, relative delay, coupling strength, and loss control the isolation, in agreement with direct time-domain simulations. The approach is general and applicable to integrated photonic, phononic, microwave, and superconducting-circuit platforms.

titles.title: Magnet-free nonreciprocal frequency conversion using sequential temporal modulation: Theory and simulations

abstracts.value: When a two-level quantum system is driven periodically with a Rabi frequency <math><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi></math> comparable to the driving frequency <math><msub><mi>ν</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></math>, the resonant transition frequency deviates from the bare energy gap—an effect known as the Bloch-Siegert shift. Observing sub-Hertz Bloch-Siegert shift is challenging due to its small energy scale and its mixing with other systematic shifts. Using a Floquet-engineered optical lattice clock, we directly observe this sub-hertz shift in ultracold atoms. We tune driving parameters to suppress micromotion and apply a self-comparison stroboscopic method to remove unwanted frequency shifts. Assisted by closed-loop feedback, we achieve high-precision results after one hour of averaging and longer integration will further improve the measurement accuracy.

titles.title: Observation of a sub-Hertz-level Bloch-Siegert shift in a Floquet-engineered optical lattice clock

Optical clocks have achieved remarkable estimated fractional frequency uncertainties reaching the $10^{-18}$ level and below, enabling applications in fundamental physics, general relativity, and geodesy. However, the challenge of verifying the international consistency of optical clocks remains critical as efforts intensify toward redefining the SI second based on an optical transition or transitions. We report on a two-month international clock comparison campaign involving seven optical clocks in four national metrology institutes (INRIM, LNE-OP, NPL, and PTB) connected via the optical fiber network established in Europe. The campaign resulted in optical frequency ratios with uncertainties ranging from $7.7\times10^{-18}$ to $6.1\times10^{-17}$. Among the results, the $^{171}$Yb$^+$(E3) clocks at NPL and PTB demonstrated agreement within an uncertainty of $7.7\times10^{-18}$, marking the first international verification of two independently developed optical clocks below one part in $10^{17}$. The operation of the $^{199}$Hg clock at LNE-OP (formerly LNE-SYRTE) resulted in frequency ratios with improved uncertainties with $^{171}$Yb$^+$(E3), $^{171}$Yb, and $^{87}$Sr optical clocks. These results provide input for the redefinition of the second and underscore how fiber-linked clock networks can advance metrology and scientific applications.

abstracts.value: In this paper, we use the Feingold-Peres model, a well-known paradigm of quantum chaos, as an example. Using semiclassical analysis and numerical simulations, we investigate the statistical properties of observables in few-body systems with chaotic classical limits and the emergence of random-matrix-theory universality. More specifically, we focus on (1) the applicability of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis in few-body systems and the dependence of its form on the effective Planck constant and (2) the existence of a universal random-matrix-theory description of observables when truncated to a small microcanonical energy window. Our results provide insights into the established field of few-body quantum chaos and help bridge it to modern perspectives, such as the general eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.

abstracts.value: Foundation models are increasingly being pursued in particle and nuclear physics, but existing approaches remain strongly tied to individual experiments through detector-specific architectures or pre-training objectives, limiting their reuse across sensing modalities. We show that a point cloud self-distillation framework yields a substantially more general sensor-level pre-training recipe. We show that the same refined architecture and objective can be independently pre-trained with minimal changes on three qualitatively different detector modalities: liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC), collider TPC, and water Cherenkov. Using 1,000 labeled images for downstream task adaptation, Panda V2 matches or exceeds specialized foundation-model baselines trained with orders of magnitude more supervision, matching state-of-the-art particle-clustering performance with 70x fewer labeled events on sPHENIX while substantially improving particle identification, and on LArTPC data matching Panda (arXiv:2512.01324) particle reconstruction with up to 1,000x fewer labels. Beyond reconstruction, simple linear probes reveal physically meaningful latent structure associated with particle causality and track curvature.

titles.title: Panda Diplomacy: Foundation Model Pre-training across Particle Imaging Detectors for High Energy and Nuclear Physics

abstracts.value: Multimodal evaluations cannot say whether a vision-language model misread an image or misreasoned about it, because every existing method for separating the two places a second model in the loop. We introduce the render ceiling, a model-free reference for benchmarks built by rendering known objects: inverting the frozen cameras and re-solving cross-view correspondence recovers exactly the answer the images support. We prove the ceiling fails only through an enumerable set of projection coincidences and certify that set empty on 2,160 rendered crystal structures, so every point of a model's deficit belongs to the model. Across fourteen vision-language models, supplying exact geometry as text lifts every model yet closes under half the gap for thirteen, while a supervised vision model with no language component reads the same images at 0.8952, above every vision-language model. The instrument exposes extraction-stage fabrication that downstream accuracy would misattribute to reasoning, yields camera-placement rules for benchmark builders, and transfers to any benchmark with an invertible forward rendering.

titles.title: Separating perception from reasoning in vision-language models: a model-free render ceiling for crystal structures

abstracts.value: Under compact symmetry, observable behavior reduces to an invariant operator algebra, but its dimension is not yet classical memory: some coordinates are dynamically frozen, some invisible to threshold tests, and some already classical. We develop an operator-algebraic theory that separates these effects through three filters. For one automaton, behavior is the Hilbert--Schmidt pairing between prefix-reachable states and suffix-observable effects, whose rank equals the real Hankel rank without controllability or observability assumptions. Maximizing this invariant over a symmetry-constrained dynamical class gives a structural capacity controlled by the symmetry commutant: its center stores isotypic populations frozen by reversible dynamics, its traceless multiplicity blocks carry movable noncommutative coordinates, dissipation removes the unary spectral loss inside those blocks, and covariant mobility releases relative populations subject to component conservation. Operational realization then determines which surviving coordinates force probabilistic states. For a fixed nontrivial invariant readout, full mobility gives an exact dichotomy in worst-case state cost: a commutative invariant algebra costs exactly its dimension, whereas a noncommutative multiplicity block raises the unrestricted cost by exactly one state. Thus noncommutativity has a one-state worst-case classical price. The known four-letter quadratic-plus-one law at trivial symmetry is the fully mobile endpoint of this principle. Schur--Weyl duality further shows that different preserved symmetries on the same tensor-power Hilbert space can change the worst memory scale from polynomial to exponential, while fixed-weight modules give an exact Catalan law at half filling, with structural capacity equal to the Catalan count minus its central-sector correction.

titles.title: Behavioral Memory under Symmetry in One-Way Quantum Automata

abstracts.value: We construct a constant-degree and constant-gap quantum expander on $n$ qubits where each unitary can be implemented by a depth-$1$ and 1D circuit of Pauli or CNOT gates. We provide two applications of this expander. First, we use it to construct a family of frustration-free 1D Hamiltonians whose ground states obey the entanglement-gap relation $S = Θ(Δ^{-1/2})$; this is believed to be optimal, but achieving it had been open. Second, we use it to provide a streaming protocol that tests for closeness to a class of 1D volume-law entangled states. Moreover, we extend our quantum expander to a constant-degree and constant-gap expander on the unitary group where each unitary is a single $T$ gate, a single $T^{\dagger}$ gate, or a depth-$1$ Clifford circuit. This implies that a random sequence of unitaries from the expander yields a gapped walk on a dense subgroup of the unitary group. This improves upon previous work by Bourgain and Gamburd which did not control the dependence of the gap on the dimension.

titles.title: Depth-1 expanders on the unitary group and applications

abstracts.value: We give a sampling problem that is solvable by shallow quantum circuits, hard for polynomial-time classical algorithms under lattice-based assumptions, and efficiently verifiable by a classical computer. The quantum sampler admits two implementations: one uses log-logarithmic-depth quantum circuits with one- and two-qubit gates, i.e., $\mathsf{QNC}^0[\log\log]$ circuits, while the other uses constant-depth quantum circuits with unbounded fan-in gates, i.e., $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits. Our construction can be seen as compiling the Learning with Errors (LWE)-based single-round proof of quantumness of Arabadjieva et al. (2025) to very low depth. The price paid for this compilation is the reliance on less standard, though well-motivated, assumptions: in addition to the lattice knowledge assumption used by Arabadjieva et al. (2025), we require a strengthened variant of the adaptive-hardcore-bit property of LWE, for which we provide supporting evidence. Unlike previous low-depth proofs of quantumness, the quantum computation here requires no mid-circuit measurements or feed-forward: it consists only of running a shallow circuit and sampling from its output distribution. This shows that shallow quantum circuits have sufficient structure to solve certain classically hard tasks whose solutions can be verified efficiently.

titles.title: Verifiable quantum advantage in extremely low depth

abstracts.value: This paper introduces QXymb, a general framework for constructing observational declarative twins of quantum circuits, and develops QILP-0, its first complete order-0 specialization. QILP-0 constructs a finite multi-valued propositional logic program from observed circuit behaviour within a declared observational scope. The pipeline traverses a declared family of quantum observables incrementally according to a reproducible structural grading and a declared observational reference horizon. Progress is quantified through reference-relative coverage against a fixed target-independent reference. Observable responses are organized through target-independent geometry, while retained latent structure is mapped deterministically back to original observable columns before symbolic processing, preserving observational semantics and provenance. Selected observable profiles are converted into a finite relation through admissible target-independent discretization. The target is used only afterwards to audit twin-admissibility and induce the declarative theory. A theory is certified as an exact observational declarative twin when it completely and correctly reconstructs the resulting finite task-conditioned discrete relation. Logical exactness is therefore separated from numerical, backend, provider, and discretization uncertainty, which is retained as audit metadata. Validation uses two complementary QML settings. Exhaustive Bars & Stripes experiments compare product and grid-CZ embeddings from 16 to 100 qubits and exercise the native-discrete branch. Low-Depth MNIST analyses all 14,708 digit-0/1 instances before and after a trained variational quantum transformation and exercises continuous discretization. In every reported relation, the induced QILP-0 theory achieves complete, conflict-free reconstruction with strict accuracy equal to one.

titles.title: QILP-0: Constructing Observational Declarative Twins of Quantum Circuits

abstracts.value: Quantum hardware is beginning to address structured combinatorial optimisation, but two steps still block practical use: mapping real operational models onto hardware-compatible instances, and converting noisy hardware output back into feasible decisions. Here we introduce a backend-agnostic computational interface that compiles the discrete decision layer of stochastic unit commitment into a move-based maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem, while retaining continuous dispatch and feasibility recovery in the classical computational layer. We validate the approach in a green hydrogen scheduling setting and deploy it on the QuEra Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor. This is the first end-to-end industrial scheduling workflow that connects real operational decisions to programmable neutral-atom hardware through a solver-agnostic MWIS representation. Across a 15-day hardware campaign on 50-node instances, hardware-generated solutions after classical refinement match or exceed the dispatch margins obtained from exact MWIS on every day. When scaling to 144 nodes, encoding quality remains stable, while the probability that the full atom array survives, rather than graph embedding, emerges as the dominant bottleneck to further scaling. Together, these results establish a hardware-compatible computational pathway toward larger problem scales, and lay the groundwork for exploring regimes in which exact classical optimisation may no longer scale efficiently.

titles.title: A Backend-Agnostic MWIS Kernel for Stochastic Unit Commitment with Neutral-Atom Hardware Validation

abstracts.value: Extracting physics information from modern particle-physics experiments requires multistage analyses implemented on top of large and highly interconnected software ecosystems. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) often produce unreliable programs for such tasks because a user request alone rarely specifies the required APIs, dependencies, and usage conventions. We organize these software relations before generation and retrieve task-relevant knowledge at inference time. Using the open-source ROOT framework as a representative and reproducible testbed, we evaluate a complete grounding system that combines hybrid retrieval over a heterogeneous software knowledge graph, skill-selected workflow examples, and execution-guided repair. On a benchmark of 275 ROOT tasks, grounding improves first-attempt execution from 58.5% to 76.0% under Claude Code orchestration and from 51.3% to 64.0% under standalone orchestration. Final success increases from 90.5% to 96.0% and from 78.9% to 90.9%, respectively, while the average generation cost per successful task increases by only 1.3% and 3.2%. The gains persist under a strong coding agent, indicating that explicit software knowledge remains valuable even when agentic scaffolding is already in place. Because the method captures software relations common to large codebases rather than facts specific to ROOT or a particular model, it should transfer to other experiment frameworks and proprietary software, especially where documentation is sparse or internal dependencies are complex.

titles.title: Reliable LLM-Generated Programs for High-Energy Physics Experiments through Graph-Grounded Software Knowledge

abstracts.value: Recently in the physics literature there have been a small, but growing, number of papers that have applied the Eynard-Orantin topological recursion procedure to spectral curves with ramification loci of infinite cardinality. However, there is a corresponding gap in the mathematics literature; indeed, it has not been checked rigorously whether the resulting infinite sums converge, or whether the resulting correlators have all the desired properties of the topological recursion. The present work aims to bridge this gap by defining topological recursion on a suitably broad class of spectral curves to cover the aforementioned physics applications and to rigorously prove that this definition has the properties one would intuitively expect. As a by-product, some interesting coincidences involving quantum curves are discovered, where two different spectral curves yield the same quantum curve, a situation that has, hitherto, not appeared in the literature.

titles.title: Topological Recursion on Spectral Curves with Infinite Ramification Loci

abstracts.value: We prove the shuffle realization for quantum affine superalgebras of types $B,C,D$ in the loop realization, in that we construct an isomorphism between each of these algebras and a suitably defined double shuffle algebra. We explicitly describe the latter shuffle algebra using certain vanishing conditions that generalize the Feigin-Odesskii wheel conditions; a novel feature is the appearance of a so-called scary wheel, which is a particular order $2$ vanishing condition involving $7$ variables. Along the way, we fully develop the theory of shrubs in super types $A$ (affine and toroidal), which are important combinatorial tools in the study of the shuffle algebras associated to toric Calabi-Yau threefolds. Our techniques also allow us to define quantum toroidal superalgebras of types $B,C,D$. More importantly, we provide a general framework to formulate and prove shuffle realizations in the wide generality of quivers with parameters.

titles.title: Scary Wheels (and Super Shrubs)

abstracts.value: Conventional quantum-code constructions encode pure logical states as pure code states, but this restriction can sacrifice performance. We show that intrinsic encoding randomness can improve optimal entanglement fidelity. We bound the loss from imposing a rank-one encoder and prove it is at most quadratic near perfect recovery after joint optimization. The optimized advantage survives small noise perturbations. An explicit noise family requires higher-rank encoders arbitrarily close to perfect recovery, with every optimal encoder mapping pure inputs to mixed code states.

titles.title: High-Rank Encoding Can Improve Approximate Quantum Error Correction
